title: Abandon
full_review:
"Abandon" is a gloomy, plodding college campus thriller that occasionally strikes an intelligent chord and rivets into real suspense before falling off into a draggy lull. The film walks a fine line between a stylized teen slasher-style movie and a moody detective story. It ultimately offers little resolution as a hollow psychodrama and fails at developing richer themes about bright young students.

Writer-director Stephen Gaghan, who won an Academy Award for his screenplay for "Traffic," mindfully captures an atmosphere of the anxious, uncertain tension of a young woman (Katie Holmes). She is days away from her final exam, does not yet have the conclusion to her thesis, and has just applied to one of the top investment firms in the country. To make her life even more nerve-wracking, she is the central figure in the investigation of her missing boyfriend (Charlie Hunnam) by a persistent and handsome detective (Benjamin Bratt).

"Abandon" attempts to portray interesting college students. Embry Larkin (Hunnam), the missing boyfriend, is a mercurial young man with innovative artistic tendencies. He produced his own opera and experimental theater. Harrison Hobart (Gabriel Mann) organizes demonstrations against "globalization." And Katie Burke (Holmes) is a very attractive, driven, self-assured young woman who came from a working-class background and knows how to dazzle a group of corporate recruiters with a steely confidence and self-understanding that is a rarity among most people.

Police detective Wade Handler (Bratt) carries a certain intrigue. His father was a teacher, and he seems to be very well read, as his bookshelves are filled with classic literature. But these details, as well as the fact that he is a semi-recovered alcoholic who has sabotaged his relationship with a woman with whom he once built a log cabin, seem to be window dressing. "Abandon" floats between the mystery and the not-so-mysterious about the missing Embry Larkin and poses the questions: Who is terrorizing Katie Burke, who will snap under academic and peer pressure, and who will turn up missing next?

It is ironic "Abandon" never probes very deeply into who Katie Burke, its central character, is. She even attends therapy sessions where her doctor ultimately tries to seduce her. The only thing that seems to be revealed about Katie is that most men are extremely attracted to her. There is reference and vague flashback sequences that show how Katie was abandoned by her father when she was a little girl. This is the film's key theme, but does not properly come to a dramatic conclusion.

Because of sexual encounters between college students and others, mild language, violence, use of marijuana, and one instance of heavy drinking, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13. (2002)
